entries.title: Germany's Alexander Zverev clinches tennis No. 1 ranking
entries.summary: Alexander Zverev is the second German man, after Boris Becker, to clinch the No. 1 spot in tennis.
entries.content:
October 29, 2026

Alexander Zverev is the second German man, after Boris Becker, to clinch the No. 1 spot in tennis.

German tennis star Alexander Zverev is set to become the new world No. 1 in tennis, capping a successful year where he won two Grand Slams.

Zverev is the second German man, after Boris Becker, to clinch the top spot in the sport. Becker reached No.1 some 35 years ago.

Zverev replaces Italy's Jannik Sinner, who previously held the world's No. 1 spot.

Zverev got there by reaching the quarter-finals of the Erste Bank Open in Vienna this week.

He is also the second-oldest first-time No. 1 ranked player after Australian John Newcombe.

"(It is) very special. To have the feeling to be on the top of the world is amazing," Zverev said.

"It is different than winning a tournament or a title, but it's such a special feeling to know that the No. 1 is going to be next to your name when the new rankings come out."

Among German female tennis players, only Steffi Graf and Angelique Kerber have achieved this in the WTA rankings.

Two Grand Slams in 2026

Zverev's career had been defined by getting close to Grand Slam titles but never quite reaching them, facing stiff competition from Sinner and Spanish talent Carlos Alcaraz.

The Hamburg-born also won a gold medal in the 2021 Olympics.

But his tennis career finally had its breakthrough this year, when he won the Grand Slam at both the French and US Opens.

Known for his consistency, he was just the ninth man to reach at least the semifinals at all four majors in the same season.

If you rely on our team for trusted reporting, please take a moment to select us as your Preferred Source on Google, so you'll always see our verified news first.

entries.title: 'Star Trek' star Patrick Stewart dies age 86
entries.summary: The Shakespearean actor landed the role of a lifetime as "Star Trek" Captain Picard. He passed away at age 86.
entries.content:
October 29, 2026

The Shakespearean actor landed the role of a lifetime as "Star Trek" Captain Picard. He passed away at age 86.

For Star Trek fans, he was the legendary Captain Picard; the British actor and director Patrick Stewart, longtime member of the Royal Shakespeare Company, died on Thursday at the age of 86 following a "brief and poignant journey" with Alzheimer's disease and Lewy body dementia, according to an official statement on his social media accounts.

In Los Angeles, California, far away from the small English village of Mirfield where he was born, Stewart achieved world fame. He was 47 years old when he landed the role of a lifetime in the legendary science fiction series Star Trek: Playing Captain Jean-Luc Picard in "Star Trek: The Next Generation," he stepped into the shoes of the legendary Captain James T. Kirk, played by William Shatner.

Stewart brought a calm, measured and distinctly British presence that quickly made Picard a fan favorite and a cult figure in the Star Trek universe. He returned to the role decades later in the spin-off series "Star Trek: Picard," which ended in 2023, proving the character's enduring appeal.

As Captain Jean-Luc Picard, he led the crew of the starship Enterprise, a spaceship with the sizeable mission: "To explore strange new worlds. To seek out new life and new civilizations" — and most importantly, "to boldly go where no man has gone before!"

In love with Shakespeare

Stewart's interest in acting was sparked in the early 1950s when a teacher asked him to recite a work by Shakespeare. His passion for Shakespeare stayed with him until the end.

His parents were far removed from the glamor of the theatrical world. His father was a highly respected officer in the British Army during World War II, but at home, he was an abusive husband, and young Patrick had to helplessly witness repeated violence against his mother. Stewart wrote about his experiences with domestic violence in The Guardian in 2009. The stage, he confessed there, seemed to him "a far safer place" than reality; he saw acting as a way to escape his home life.

Patrick began acting at the age of 12. At 16, he left school early and, thanks to a scholarship, studied acting in Bristol, England. Along the way, he worked as a journalist. In 1965, he became an official member of the Royal Shakespeare Company, and remained with the theather company from 1966 to 1982. Such was his passion for the great English playwright and lyricist that he even shared his sonnets on his Twitter account during the 2020 coronavirus pandemic.

Stewart dazzled the theater world with his own stage adaptation of Charles Dickens' 1843 tale "A Christmas Carol." He played more than 30 roles himself. After its 1987 premiere in Stewart's hometown of Mirfield, the one-man show became a critics' favorite and a long-running hit on Broadway in New York.

'Star Trek' offer from Hollywood

In the same year, Stewart went from being a stage actor to an international TV star. Star Trek producer Robert Justman offered him the role of Captain Jean-Luc Picard, one of the main characters in a new edition of the popular TV series "Star Trek: The Next Generation."

The successful Shakespearean hesitated. Until then, he had never worked in Hollywood. But his agent encouraged him to accept the role, Stewart recalled in a 2020 interview with the German newspaper Die Welt. "You can accept the offer as a start for now. It won't be a big deal, you can't revive a series as iconic as Star Trek anyway."

Adventures in the universe

But his agent was to be proven wrong: Stewart led the Starship Enterprise through its galactic adventures for seven seasons and four full-length feature films. The TV series had astronomical success on Earth in a very short time.



At first, the producers were at odds as to whether Stewart's British accent could really fit the role of commander of a US starship in the 24th century, but it soon became impossible to imagine the series without the subtly diplomatic Captain Picard, who often quoted Shakespeare while at the helm. It seemed as if all the time he had spent as a Shakespearean actor had prepared him to command the Enterprise, Stewart once remarked with a wink. When the cult series ended in 1994, he had ruled out ever returning to the Enterprise's command center. 

In 2010, the actor was knighted by the Queen of England. Stewart considered it the greatest honor of his career to stand alongside acting greats such as Sir Laurence Olivier and Sir Alec Guinness.

Beyond the screen, Stewart has long used his voice for social and human rights causes. In recent years, he has drawn attention to issues such as violence against women, age discrimination and the protection of children.

A short-lived retirement

In a June 2020 interview, "Playboy" asked the New York resident whether he was considering retiring from acting. "Never! That would mean giving up my life," replied Stewart, who was approaching his 80th birthday at the time. He was filming the second of three seasons of "Star Trek: Picard." The series ends with a final episode in which the retired Starfleet admiral makes his last appearance. In the series, Picard retires to his family vineyard in France but is drawn back into space to confront new threats to the Federation.

This series also showcases Stewart's affection for his pit bull, Ginger. In "Star Trek: Picard," Picard also has a pit bull, a loyal four-legged companion named Number One — a deliberate reference to Stewart's real-life love of the breed. For his efforts to combat prejudice against pit bulls and to support their adoption, Stewart was honored by the US animal welfare organization ASPCA, among others.

In 2024, he published his memoir "Making it So." In it, he recounts his passion for theater and his love of Shakespeare.

Now, at the age of 86, the British actor has finally departed for another galaxy. Farewell, Patrick Stewart!

Translated from German by Sarah Hucal.

entries.title: Justice for Maya women in Guatemala, girls back in school in India, restored land in Mali: The UN has named its 2026 SDG Action Award winners
entries.summary: Champions of indigenous women's rights in Guatemala, girls' education in India, and restored farmland in Mali all featured among the winners of UN's SDG Action Awards.
entries.content:
October 29, 2026

Champions of indigenous women's rights in Guatemala, girls' education in India, and restored farmland in Mali all featured among the winners of UN's SDG Action Awards.

A legal aid group for Indigenous women in Guatemala, a movement of village mothers in rural India, and a Malian entrepreneur who restores farmland have won this year's UN SDG Action Awards.

The winners were announced at the ninth Heroes of Tomorrow awards ceremony in Rome, Italy, run by the UN SDG Action Campaign. They were chosen from more than 7,000 entries from 190 countries.

Nine finalists were shortlisted for three categories: resilience, creativity and changemaker.

Justice for Maya women

The Resilience Award went to the Women's Justice Initiative. Many indigenous women in Guatemala face high rates of violence, poverty and discrimination, made worse by language barriers and a lack of access to information. The initiative helps women and girls get access to justice and lead change in their communities. According to the organization, more than 16,000 women and girls have participated.

"I accept the UN SDG Action Award in the honour of the Maya Kaqchikel women and girls in Guatemala who are building a more just future for their communities. Ending violence against women requires all of us. Only together, we can build a future where every woman and girl lives with dignity and realizes her full potential," said Viviana Patal, the initiative's legal director.

Keeping girls in school in India

The Creativity Award was given to Mothers of Courage, a grassroots campaign that aims to keep girls in education in rural India. Its organizers say more than 1.2 million people have joined and pledged to keep their daughters in education and to prevent early marriage.

"This award today belongs to all the mothers in those villages, all the women leaders, who are working hard to change the destinies of their daughters and their daughters-in-law," said Khushboo Awasthi, Mothers of Courage's chief curator.

"Together, let's create a world where no girl ever has to negotiate for her right to dream and to aspire and to thrive."

Trees and livelihoods in Mali

The Changemaker Award when to Malian entrepreneur Rokiatou Traore. Her organization, Herou Alliance, helps women and small farmers bring worn-out land back to life by planting trees alongside their crops. The trees also help farmers generate extra revenue, allowing them to sell products from moringa and other valuable trees.

"Receiving this award means a lot to me. It is a reminder of why I started this journey," said Traore. "I invite you all to join us, to plant more trees, to empower more women, and above all, to create a future full of opportunities for communities for today and for future generations."

The UN Trust Fund to End Violence against Women and Girls received an honorable mention. Speaking about the award, President of the Organization of Women's Freedom in Iraq Jannat Al Ghezi paid a tearful tribute to its founder Yanar Mohammed, who was assassinated outside her home in Baghdad in March.

'Be that change'

UN Assistant Secretary-General Michelle Muschett said the finalists "remind us that the future is something we create together and that each of us has the power to help shape it and open doors for the next generations."

"When they tell you that one person cannot make a difference, prove them wrong," UN SDG Action Campaign Director Marina Ponti told the audience. "Change has always begun with people who refused to accept that the world could not be different. So be courageous. Be persistent. Be that change."

How are the awards organized?

A panel of 20 judges from UN leadership, government, civil society, the arts, business and youth activism chose the winners. They included UN Development Programme Administrator Alexander De Croo, Oxfam International Executive Director Amitabh Behar, and Otto Group Vice President Tobias Wollermann.

The awards are run by the UN SDG Action Campaign, a special initiative of the UN Secretary-General. The campaign supports the UN Sustainable Development Goals, 17 targets adopted by member states that cover areas including poverty, hunger, education, gender equality and climate protection.

The awards are supported by Italy's Foreign Ministry and Germany's Ministry for Economic Cooperation and Development.

Editor's Note: DW Director General Barbara Massing was a member of the 20-person jury panel.

entries.title: Berlin's Elif Eralp under fire over Der Spiegel interview
entries.summary: Left candidate Elif Eralp has sparked controversy after Der Speigel reported she was advised against mentioning a pro-Palestinian activist for fear of reprisals against her family.
entries.content:
Germany

Berlin's Left leader Elif Eralp under fire over Der Spiegel interview

October 29, 2026

Left candidate Elif Eralp has sparked controversy after Der Speigel reported she was advised against mentioning a pro-Palestinian activist for fear of reprisals against her family.

Elif Eralp, the candidate on course to become the next mayor of Berlin, sparked controversy on Thursday after having unintentionally aired personal security fears that appeared to be linked to pro-Palestinian activists in the city.

The controversy came about based on internal remarks that were part of her interview with the German news magazine Der Spiegel.

Eralp, whose Left Party (Die Linke) came out on top in local elections in Berlin last month, appeared to suggest in remarks made during an internal authorization process for an interview that she gave to Der Spiegel that she couldn't make references to a particular pro-Palestinian activist out of fear for her own safety.

"I can't put myself and my family in danger for Der Spiegel," the magazine cites her as having written in a Word Document edit, which was inadvertently sent back to the reporters.

"What do we do now? Cancel the whole interview?" she is cited as having asked her press officer and other party colleagues, while stating in another remark, "I should never have agreed to this interview."

Elif Eralp under pressure to clearly label out threats she sees

In the Der Spiegel interview, which was conducted on Monday in Eralp's office in Berlin's House of Representatives, the 45-year-old was asked about allegations of antisemitism that have been leveled at members of her socialist party.

Those accusations came about after at least two instances where people with questionable backgrounds showed up to celebrate after Eralp's party won elections in the city state last month.

For instance, the Left Party election celebration in the Berlin district of Neukölln was attended by a controversial pro-Palestinian activist associated with the Popular Front for the Liberation of Palestine (PFLP), which is classified as a terrorist organization by the European Union.

In the past, Ibrahim Ibrahim has described Yahya Sinwar, the former head of Hamas in Gaza, widely regarded as the mastermind behind the deadly terror attack on Israel on October 7, 2023, as a "martyr" and a "hero." He has since rejected accusations of antisemitism and of supporting terrorism or Hamas.

Asked by Der Spiegel whether she was referring to the Ibrahim incident, Eralp initially responded with a "yes." But she later returned the interview transcript to the magazine with the question crossed out and the comment regarding her and her family's safety.

In Germany, it is standard practice for an interviewee to review and approve direct quotations with media outlets before the interview is published.

In notes included in the approved version of the transcript, which Der Spiegel believes were left in by accident, Eralp wrote that Berlin police had previously advised her not to comment on specific individuals.

Der Spiegel on why it published the notes

That Eralp chose to conceal her concerns publicly led some politicians to ask whether she was the right person to be the mayor of Berlin.

Der Spiegel wrote in its story:

"There were reasons not to publish – Eralp's security concerns first and foremost," the magazine wrote. "But the political importance of her notes outweighed them. Der Spiegel believes that the public should know."

It added that the story begs the question: "Can a woman who is too scared to name a terrorist sympathizer in an interview be responsible for the security of all Berliners?"

SPD, Greens also weigh in

Rival politicians weighed in, including from the Social Democrats (SPD) and Greens, with whom the Left Party is due to conduct coalition talks in Berlin next month.

"I would advise my party to distance itself from an alliance with the Left Party," said the SPD's Karl Lauterbach, who rose to prominence as Germany's health minister during the Covid-19 pandemic.

"Further talks about a coalition with this party should be out of the question for any social democrat," added SPD internal affairs spokesman Sebastian Fiedler.

Katharina Dröge, the leader of the Green Party's parliamentary grouping, asked in the Süddeutsche Zeitung newspaper, "Will [Eralp] continue to let herself be influenced by those in her own ranks who are close to criminal groups and who tolerate threats and intimidation towards their own lead candidate? Or will she manage to give a clear and tough response?"

The chairman of the Central Council of Jews in Germany, Josef Schuster, warned: "The SPD and the Greens have a duty not to hand governmental responsibility for Berlin and for the security of the Jewish community to the Left Party" and claimed the story showed that "the Left Party is incapable of distancing itself from terrorist sympathizers and antisemites."

Eralp issues tough response, hits out at critics

Eralp hit back later on Thursday, slamming a "truly toxic debate," vowing not to be intimidated and promising a tough stance "against organized crime, against organizations that glorify violence, against violence, against terror."

She said she wouldn't comment on the specifics of the Der Spiegel story but insisted that she would "ensure the security of all Berliners."

Eralp also received backing from the vice-president of the German parliament and veteran Left Party colleague Bodo Ramelow, who criticized the Der Spiegel story as "more than questionable."

He said the reporting "targeted a person who feels vulnerable and made them even more vulnerable." He said internal communications had been used to depict the "anachronistic cliché" of a "weak woman."

Edited by: Roshni Majumdar

entries.title: Iraq: Life sentences for 3 French 'Islamic State' suspects
entries.summary: The three were among 47 French "Islamic State" suspects transferred from Syrian detention. So far, ten French nationals have received prison terms after being convicted of belonging to the group.
entries.content:
October 29, 2026

The three were among 47 French "Islamic State" suspects transferred from Syrian detention. So far, ten French nationals have received prison terms after being convicted of belonging to the group.

Three French nationals on Thursday received sentences of life imprisonment in Iraq after being convicted of joining the so-called "Islamic State" terror group.

The criminal court in Baghdad sentence Charly S., Kamal M, and Amir A. to life terms in prison which amounts to 20 years of imprisonment in Iraq.

What more do we know?

The trio were found guilty of "the crime of joining the terrorist Islamic State organisation and of having contributed, together with members of the group, to spreading terror," an AFP correspondent said.

Tuesday saw another six French nationals from the same group sentenced to life in prison and a seventh to 15 years for belonging ​to the Islamist militant group.

All of the French nationals sentenced thus far belong to a group of 47 French nationals who were transferred from detention in Syria last year.

The 'Islamic State's' years of terror in Syria and Iraq

The militant group carried out a campaign of terror as it sought to establish a self-proclaimed caliphate in Iraq and Syria from 2014 under its leader, Abu Bakr al-Baghdadi.

Thousands of foreign nationals from across the world joined the group, which carried out mass executions and other atrocities, many of them filmed and shared on social media platforms.

Among its most heinous crimes was the capture and killing of thousands of Yazidis in Iraq’s northern Sinjar region. Many Yazidi women and children were forced into sexual slavery and other forms of enslavement.

In 2014, IS also captured and killed hundreds of Iraqi military cadets at Camp Speicher in Iraq's Tikrit in 2014, much of the massacre filmed and shared on social media.

The terror group also carried out a series of executions of Western journalists and aid workers in highly choreographed videos as part of its media campaign.

Iraq, backed by US-led forces, proclaimed victory over IS in 2017, and along with the Kurdish-led Syrian Democratic Forces would go on to ultimately defeat the group territorially in Syria two years later.

The remaining fighters were eventually cornered and defeated in Baghouz in Syria's eastern Deir Ezzor, near the Iraqi border in March, 2019.

entries.title: EU seeks 'highest level' ties with Canada in Montreal summit
entries.summary: European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said EU seeks "association without accession" for Canada, after EU members snub "associate member" designation.
entries.content:
Canada

EU seeks 'highest level' ties with Canada in Montreal summit

October 29, 2026

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said EU seeks "association without accession" for Canada, after EU members snub "associate member" designation.

European Union and Canadian leaders are set to meet at a special Canada-EU summit to discuss critical policies like artificial inteligence (AI), climate, energy and ⁠security.

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said on Thursday, ahead of the summit, which begins on Friday, that the EU will continue to explore Canada's prospects for becoming the bloc's first "associate member."

But despite her comments, the summit's declaration is expected to exclude the term "associate member," a move pushed by Germany and other members.

"Our idea is simple: it is an association without accession," Von der Leyen clarified. "We can build a partnership that comes closer to membership than anything we have done before."

"We both want to bring our relationship to the highest level possible," von der Leyen added.

Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney had said this week he wasn't concerned about the  "associate member" status, or "specific names" to be given to the new alliance with the EU.

"What matters is the difference that it will make to the lives of Canadians," Carney added.

Canada's EU ties are part of a broader strategy, expert tells DW

Ottawa's quest for deeper ties to Europe is seen as a move to reduce its reliance on the US since President Donald Trump imposed tariffs on a range of Canadian goods.

Frederic Merand, political expert on EU-Canada relations at the University of Montreal, spoke to DW about how the summit serves as "political impetus" to improve the bilateral trade relationship and to free Canada of its reliance on the US.

"It's not going to happen, over time, overnight. And every time we move closer to the Europeans, we realize how dependent we are on the US and how also vulnerable we are to, for example, us retaliation," Merand said.

But he added that courting the EU is also part of a broader strategy "to reinvent the Canadian economy, to create a single market, to attract more investment," as well as to diversify our partnerships with China, India and also other parts of the world.

The EU is "a natural partner" to work with, Merand said, given its existing free trade agreement with Canada, in addition to the close historical and cultural ties between the two partners.

What's on the agenda for the summit?

An EU official, speaking on condition of anonymity, told AFP that Canada and the EU sought to align policies in areas such as climate, energy and artificial intelligence, allowing Ottawa to participate in some EU programs.

Canada has critical minerals needed for green technologies such as batteries and wind turbines, something for which Europe normally relies on China.

But Canada is in need of major infrastructure investment to develop its mining industry.

There are hopes that the summit can result in a plan for the European Investment Bank to back Canadian critical mineral projects.

EU and Canadian leaders are also looking into a digital trade deal that can allow for faster and cheaper online transactions.

Additionally, Canada could be allowed to participate in the EU's Erasmus youth program, which allows university students to spend a semester abroad.

entries.title: Israel election: Authorities dispute Netanyahu’s fraud claims
entries.summary: Benjamin Netanyahu's Likud claims large-scale foreign involvement in the elections led by Qatar and Turkey, with Israel’s authorities so far refuting the claims.
entries.content:
October 29, 2026

Benjamin Netanyahu's Likud claims large-scale foreign involvement in the elections led by Qatar and Turkey, with Israel’s authorities so far refuting the claims.

Israel woke up on Thursday to allegations by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's Likud party that foreign actors may have sought to influence voter mobilization efforts in Arab communities during this week's legislative election. 

No'am Sohlberg, the Supreme Court judge who heads Israel's Central Election Committee, sent a letter to Israel's internal security agency Shin Bet to look into the Likud's claims. 

According to Likud's statement, Arab parties Ra'am and the Joint List — which received a record share of the vote, mostly due to unprecedented turnout in communities of Arab and Palestinians with Israeli citizenship — allegedly used "severe criminal offenses" to spur voters to go to the polls, including bribery, threats and other forms of election fraud.

"Severe suspicions were brought to my attention about improper intervention in the elections by foreign funding by outside actors that act against the Israeli interest," Sohlberg wrote in the letter, adding that he was "unable to testify" as to whether the allegations are true.

"The elections in the State of Israel were stolen by Arab parties that support terrorism and the elimination of the Jewish state," Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's party claimed in a statement. His own coalition lost seats, leaving both the prime minister and his opponents short of a majority — unless they were to work with one or both of the Arab parties.

Likud and other right-wing figures pointed to the unusually high turnout in Arab communities, reports of organized transportation to polling stations and concerns over foreign-funded voter mobilization campaigns as grounds for requesting an investigation. They argue that a formal review is necessary to maintain public confidence in the electoral process, regardless of whether wrongdoing is ultimately found.

Authorities refute allegations

Israel's elections are administered by the Central Election Committee, a body comprising representatives of parliamentary parties and chaired by a Supreme Court justice. Large-scale election fraud has historically been rare, although disputes over campaign conduct and voting procedures regularly arise.

Israeli police said there is no evidence to support Likud's claims, neither "investigative” nor "informative.”

"Election day went with a minority of irregular incidents in the area of election integrity, also compared to other elections," it said in a statement.

A high-ranking Central Election Committee official, too, denied the allegations.

"We don't have any basis for claims of 'stolen elections,'" Dean Livne, the Committee's acting director general, told Israeli public broadcaster Kan 11, adding that the committee received "claims rather than evidence" from Likud and other parties.

Gadi Eisenkot, Netanyahu's main competitor and the head of the Yashar party, blamed the Israeli leader for leading an "improper influence operation" to cast doubt on the elections and create what he called "a fictive delegitimization" for the next parliament.

However, Eisenkot, also called for Likud's allegation of electoral fraud to be investigated.

The religious Muslim Ra'am party denied any involvement and said it would cooperate with any investigation.

Qatar released a statement denying any involvement in the Israeli elections, calling them "false propaganda aimed at dragging Qatar's name into Israel's political conflicts."

The controversy comes against the backdrop of growing polarization in Israeli politics and increasing public distrust between rival political camps.

Likud's motivation could be to decrease the Arab influence on Israeli politics, according to Amira Halperin, a senior fellow at the Palm Beach Center for Democracy and Policy Research. "The Arab votes were very, very important in this election," she said.

Such allegations could also hurt the public's trust in the election process Halperin argued: "We need to be cautious about predicting a failure of the democratic system."

Shin Bet head in focus

Israeli media reports have suggested that some of the concerns cited by Likud were based on intelligence assessments examined by the Shin Bet, though the agency has not publicly confirmed the details of any such findings.

Public broadcaster Kan reported the suspicions' extent as "relatively small," citing sources familiar with the Shin Bet investigation. Israeli daily Ha'aretz, too, quoted sources familiar with the allegations as saying the reports are "being blown out of proportion.”

David Zini, the head of the agency, said on election day that the elections in Israel are "safe, sound and supervised," adding that the Elections Committee and Israeli police are "successfully" preventing anyone from hurting it.

Zini's appointment earlier this year was criticized by opposition figures, who questioned both his qualifications for the role and Netanyahu's motives in selecting him. Supporters of the appointment rejected those criticisms, arguing that Zini's military experience and security background made him suitable for the position.

Separately, the Shin Bet, has been involved in investigating several of Netanyahu's closest aides on allegations of undisclosed ties to Qatar. Those investigations are unrelated to the current election allegations.

Pre-planned tactics?

Israeli outlet N12 has reported that in the weekend before the elections that Likud officials were discussing potential election-integrity complaints ahead of voting, although no evidence of actual irregularities had been presented at that stage, with a focus on Arab and Palestinian communities .

"They sat and brainstormed to find creative ideas of how to complain about this issue," said Daphna Liel, the reporter who broke the story.

Historic turnout

Arab and Palestinian participation in this week's election was unprecedented, with turnout jumping from around 50% in 2022 to about 80% in 2026, according to reports in Israel.

Arab voter participation has fluctuated significantly in recent decades. Turnout has often been influenced by debates within Arab society over whether participation in national elections can effectively advance the interests of Arab citizens, who comprise roughly 20% of Israel's population. The exceptionally high turnout in this election was widely seen as a sign of renewed political mobilization.

This resulted in huge success forthe Joint List and Ra'am, with 11 and eight parliament seats, respectively, in comparison to six and four in the 2022 election. Both parties have already voiced their willingness to cooperate with Israel's Zionist opposition to replace Netanyahu.

Most parties in Israel's Zionist opposition promised not to join a coalition with Arab parties ahead of the elections, with the exception of left-wing Zionist party "The Democrats” (HaDemocratim).

On election day, there were also allegations over "systematic delays" in voting in Arab and Palestinian polling stations, according to Adalah, an Israeli-Palestinian NGO for the legal rights of the Arab minority in Israel.

entries.title: India increases growth forecast for fiscal year
entries.summary: India's Ministry of Finance has increased its growth forecasts for the current fiscal year. But it also warned about inflation, particularly for fuel and energy, amid continued instability in the Middle East.
entries.content:
India

India increases growth forecast for fiscal year

October 29, 2026

India's Ministry of Finance has increased its growth forecasts for the current fiscal year. But it also warned about inflation, particularly for fuel and energy, amid continued instability in the Middle East.

India's Ministry of Finance expects India's economy to grow at a pace of 7.3% in the current fiscal year based on its latest assessment of current data, it said in its October economic review. 

The estimate is a slight increase on the previous forecast of 7.1%.

India's current fiscal year, known as FY27, runs from April 1, 2026 to March 31, 2027.

The report contrasted these figures with global growth predictions of nearer 3%, saying "India's growth momentum, by comparison, has held firm."

The ministry said growth in various key indicators like energy consumption, port traffic, goods and services tax (GST) collections, and car sales had accelerated in the previous quarter.

Inflation, fueled by El Nino and geopolitics, poses a threat

However, the ministry also warned of continued inflationary pressure and pressure on the rupee currency, as well as downside risks from the El Nino weather phonemenon that could threaten soil moisture ahead of the winter sowing season. 

It said that external factors like oil prices and "global uncertainties" — seemingly a reference at least in part to the instablity in the Middle East — continued to pressure the rupee's value and pose inflationary risks.

Consumer price inflation (CPI), the wholesale price index (WPI), food cost prices and fuel and power prices were all rising month for month, albeit at very different rates.

The CPI was up 5.54% year-on-year in September, but the WPI had risen more sharply at 11.39%. Food index inflation was up by 8% in rural areas, and a slightly more modest 7.18% in urban centers.

But, as in many other countries, fuel and power costs increases were in an entirely different league, at 25.85% inflation in September 2026 comapred to the same month a year earlier, prior to the outbreak of fighting in the Middle East.

Ministry says FX reserves ample, rupee's decline appears manageable

Although it has been a comparatively slow decline, the rupee has been consistently losing value against the US dollar over the past five years, threatening the country's relative purchasing power internationally. This slide has picked up pace in the last 15 months or so.

But the ministry pointed to foreign exchange reserves worth some $721 billion and said that India was "well-positioned" to weather such risks and sustain its expansionary trajectory..

entries.title: China leaders demand more loyalty and more initiative
entries.summary: The CCP session emphasized internal discipline — as expected, but left the question of Xi Jinping's successor unanswered. The party seems anxious of any instability as geopolitics heats up and China's economy cools down.
entries.content:
China

China leaders demand more loyalty and more initiative

October 29, 2026

The CCP session emphasized internal discipline — as expected, but left the question of Xi Jinping's successor unanswered. The party seems anxious of any instability as geopolitics heats up and China's economy cools down.

The top echelon of the Chinese Communist Party (CCP) held a four-day session behind closed doors in Beijing this week, with the talks focusing on strict leadership and discipline inside the ruling party.

Xi Jinping, who is both the CCP's general secretary and the head of state in China, signaled he would not only deepen the existing anti-corruption effort, but also ensure that party officials demonstrate more loyalty and more initiative at all levels.

According to the press release published on Thursday, the committee published a resolution praising the leadership and Xi Jinping for "enormous political courage and strong sense of responsibility" in tackling the issues of corruption and the weakening of the Party's governance.

The statement emphasized the need to "consistently advance comprehensive and strict Party leadership."

China's leadership fears instability

Kerry Brown, head of the Lau China Institute at King's College London, says Xi wants to minimize potential sources of instability.

Amid the current international tensions and the internal problems in China, including economic difficulties, Xi is pursuing his anti-corruption campaign and by demanding loyalty. "This is just going to intensify because if [the CCP] isn't disciplined and united, the party believes that it will go the same way as everywhere else in the world at the moment and become disunited and unstable," Brown told DW.

'Two-faced' party members targeted by Xi

Xi also recently spoke of the necessity to identify and remove "two-faced functionaries" from the political system.

In his speech, which was published in mid-October by the party's Qiushi Magazine, Xi referred to people professing loyalty to the central leadership while working against its instructions and following their own "individualistic" goals. The Chinese president described them as "political opportunists." He also criticized party officials pretending to be "nice guys," as in, those who use harmony as an excuse to stand aside when problems arise.

Brown points out that China's political system is now facing a crucial dilemma: If officials at all levels are now indeed expected to show innovation and courage in solving problems, the party's control could grow weak. This could, in turn, boost corruption.

However, if CCP leaders lean more on the "strict Party leadership" aspect and ramp up the pressure on the rank-and-file, there is also the danger of suppressing initiative. This could go beyond the party itself and could even affect the military.

The party is "very, very risk averse," Brown points out.

China 'kind of works' in a messy world

Chong Ja Ian, a political scientist at the National University of Singapore, notes that party functionaries under Xi only have a limited space to make their own decisions.

Taking this into account, the party's push for individuals to show initiative is not necessarily a major issue.

"I believe Xi would like for the officials to act proactively and decisively by conducting specific tasks; but he still doesn't want them thinking for themselves so much that they can question the agenda he prescribed. The 'proactivity' demanded by Xi is limited to the implementation, not decision-making," he told DW.

Brown adds that Xi seems to be ready to sacrifice a certain amount of operational flexibility to gain more control and stability.

"As long as you have unity, you live for another day, right? But if you have disunity, you probably die the same day," he told DW.

This approach "kind of works," at least at the moment, he added.

"It's not like the Chinese economy is disastrous. It's not great, but it's not disastrous. In any case, look at the outside world. It's a mess."

Who will succeed Xi Jinping?

Outside observers are also focusing on Xi's future and possible successors for the 73-year-old leader.

For now, Xi seems to be firmly in control. It is highly likely that he would be confirmed as the party's general secretary next fall, and could stay in that position until 2032.

This is due to the changes pushed by Xi in 2018, which removed term limits for state and party leaders.

Both analysts told DW that the issue of succession plays a major role in Xi's push towards internal stability.

"There's always a danger of differences in the party fragmenting it, especially when the question of succession comes up," says Brown. "And even though we don't expect to see a successor anytime soon, you know, there's going to be speculation about who might succeed Xi."

"He can't go on forever," he added.

Political scientist Chong Ja Ian says that Xi currently holds all the power. Therefore, the CCP leader could be afraid of his authority being undermined if he named a successor ahead of time.

"On the other hand, a failure to make preparations on time could create a power vacuum that can cause major instability," he told DW. "To solve this dilemma, the current leader needs to have both the necessary self-confidence and the readiness to take a step back — just like his predecessors did. But not everyone has that kind of confidence."

This text was originally published in Chinese.

Edited by: Darko Janjevic, Emmy Sasipornkarn

entries.content:
Germany

Germany seeks new head of state

October 29, 2026

The question of who should become Germany's new presiden is becoming pressing. Many want to see Germany's first female head of state. Chancellor Friedrich Merz is keeping his cards close to his chest.

Wanted: A new head of state — female, male, or other. Requirements: German citizen, entitled to vote, minimum age 40. Please apply as soon as possible! Availability starting January 30, 2027; job starts March 19, 2027.

This is not an official job posting, but Germany's federal government is indeed looking for someone to fill the nation's highest office. Having already served two terms, current President Frank-Walter Steinmeier is no longer eligible for another, leaving the position open for a successor. Many feel that it is time for Germany's first-ever female head of state.

"The person should have a certain level of public recognition, be politically unbiased, capable of bringing people together, approachable and a reasonably good [public] speaker," political scientist Ursula Münch told DW.

In Germany, a federal parliamentary republic, the president serves as head of state and a representative of the country as well as someone who embodies moral authority for the nation. Unlike in the US, France, or Russia, the president does not wield extensive political power or direct government affairs.

Steinmeier was nominated by his own party, the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD), in 2009. However, once elected via a convention of parliamentarians and state electors, a president-elect has to suspend their party membership in order to serve in the office apolitically. This time, it is Chancellor Friedrich Merz's center-right Christian Democrats (CDU), the senior partner in the coalition government with the SPD and the conservative Christian Social Union (CSU), which has the right to nominate a candidate.

Political scientist Münch said that "the three parties must agree on a person who is acceptable for all three." Since the convention that will select Steinmeier's successor is currently controlled by these three parties and their delegates, it is very likely that whomever Merz nominates will be elected.

Will Germany soon have its first female president?

"Well, I would really like it to be a woman this time. We've had 12 male federal presidents since 1949 — it's about time for a woman. But if the right man were to be nominated, I'd be fine with that too," said Münch. According to an August survey conducted by the Forsa polling institute for the RTL television network, about 74% of German respondents say they don't care whether it's a man or a woman. Another 19% explicitly want a woman, while 5% prefer a man.

Ilse Aigner, president of the Bavarian State Parliament in Munich, appears to have a good chance. Aigner is a member of the smallest party in the coalition, the Bavarian CSU, and is considered a unifying figure. She also has experience in government in Berlin, having served as agricultural minister at the federal level. She enjoys strong support within her Bavarian CSU party, whose leader Markus Söder recently said: "It would be tremendous if she became federal president."

Even members of the opposition Greens and the SPD are full of praise for Aigner's candidacy. "What are we actually waiting for? Surely Ilse Aigner has long since secured a majority across party lines?" asked SPD parliamentary group leader Matthias Miersch recently. However, Merz, who is friends with Aigner, has remained tight-lipped so far — possibly also because Aigner is not a member of Merz's party, but rather of its smaller sister party, the CSU.

Several female presidential candidates

Other potential successors from the CDU membership have been mentioned: Bundestag President Julia Klöckner, former Defense Minister Annegret Kramp-Karrenbauer and Education Minister Karin Prien. Hesse's state premier, Boris Rhein, is also a possible candidate. In recent days, another name has been making the rounds: lawyer Ines Claus, who serves as CDU's parliamentary group leader in Hesse and deputy party chair at the federal level — and is largely unknown.

However, rumors that she would be nominated were swiftly shot down by the chancellor. Sources close to Merz emphasized that he has so far "neither made a decision nor put forward a proposal." There are "a number of suitable" options, sources added.

The president is elected every five years by the Federal Convention, which comprises all 630 members of the Bundestag and an equal number of electors who represent the state parliaments. Among them are also prominent figures from the spheres of culture, science, sports and society. The candidate who receives more than 631 votes goes on to assume office. The governing parties — the CDU/CSU and the SPD — have a combined total of 682 votes, a comfortable majority.

Presidential role key amid polarization and crisis

The office of the president is often underestimated as merely a ceremonial role. Yet, as an authority standing above the political parties, this person wields considerable political, legal and moral influence. This is especially true in times of political polarization and international crises. While the president does not govern like a chancellor, he or she represents Germany both at home and abroad.

"From a constitutional perspective, the federal president is enormously important. For example, in a political crisis, he could decide whether it makes more sense to dissolve the Bundestag or to advocate for a minority government," explained political scientist Münch. In addition, he reviews and signs laws proposed by politicians.

What happens next?

The federal chancellor and CDU chairman has an interest in an orderly process, say sources close to the government. The "first milestone" will be the meetings of the CDU Presidium and Executive Board on November 9. Until then, discussions will be held with the state chairpersons of the CDU and the CSU. Sources made it clear that the SPD and the Greens will also be consulted, "since the election of the federal president should have broad support across the democratic spectrum."

That is how political scientist Münch sees it: "I still consider the question open, with a slight edge for CSU candidate Ilse Aigner." But there could still be a real surprise, she added.

This article was originally published in German.
